title: Complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD) | NHS inform
text:
Complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD)
Complex post traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD) happens when people experience repeated traumatic events. For example, violence, neglect or abuse. It can affect both adults and children.
Symptoms of CPTSD
The symptoms of complex PTSD are similar to the symptoms of
PTSD
but may include:
feelings of shame or guilt
difficulty controlling your emotions
feeling detached from thoughts, feelings and memories – this is known as dissociation
physical symptoms – like headaches, dizziness, chest pains and stomach aches
distancing yourself from friends and family
relationship difficulties
destructive or risky behaviour – like self-harm, alcohol misuse or drug abuse
feeling very angry or distrustful of the world
constant feelings of emptiness or hopelessness
feeling as if you’re damaged or worthless
feeling as if you’re different to other people
feeling like nobody can understand what happened to you
suicidal thoughts
Diagnosing CPTSD
You’ll likely see a specialist mental health professional like a psychologist or psychiatrist. They’ll normally complete a clinical assessment with you to understand more about your symptoms. They’ll consider how your symptoms affect you to allow before a diagnosis of CPTSD is made.
Treatment for CPTSD
You may find standard treatments for PTSD helpful. But many people with complex PTSD need more long-term, intensive support to recover.
You may be offered psychological therapies used to treat PTSD like trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). Where appropriate, medications may also be considered as part of your treatment.
As part of your treatment you should also be offered support for other problems you may experience, like depression, drug and alcohol use or dissociation. The treatment you’re offered may depend on what’s available in your local area.
What causes CPTSD?
CPTSD can be caused by different traumatic events. Some examples include:
childhood abuse, neglect or abandonment
ongoing domestic violence or abuse
repeatedly witnessing violence or abuse
being forced or manipulated into prostitution (trading sex)
torture, kidnapping or slavery
Who’s more at risk of CPTSD?
CPTSD may be more likely if the:
traumatic event happened early in life
trauma was caused by someone close to you
experienced trauma for a long time
have experienced more than one trauma
Living with CPTSD
Try our PTSD and CPTSD self help guide which aims to help you:
consider whether you’re experiencing symptoms of PTSD or CPTSD
understand more about PTSD and CPTSD
think about ways to manage or recover from PTSD or CPTSD
The guide is based on theory and evidence regarding PTSD and CPTSD, and Trauma-Focused Cognitive Therapy (TF-CT). TF-CT aims to help people who have experienced trauma and adversity to make sense of what they’ve experienced, and become less distressed and affected by it.

Further support for CPTSD
There are charities that provide peer support and advice for PTSD.
For example:
Combat Stress
– a military charity specialising in helping ex-servicemen and women
Rape Crisis
Scotland – a Scottish charity providing a range of services for people who have experienced sexual violence
Victim Support
Scotland– providing support and information to people affected by crime
CRUSE Scotland
– a charity providing support and information for people who have experienced bereavement
